text: Smoother in modern eras: towns no longer rebuild themselves one by one when nothing under them changed. Tibet and the Andes keep snow on their high peaks, not across the whole dry plateau.

Zoomed out, Earth slowly turns about its real axis (stops while you touch it), and the Moon, Sun and planets show where they really are right now. Tap any map name, ancient sea, planet or storm for its card and Wikipedia link; storms show their path and where they're headed, at their real sizes. Clouds drift with the wind belts.

All 1,270 UNESCO World Heritage Sites: each appears on the globe the year it was inscribed (gold cultural, green natural, blue mixed, red in danger), 224 historic sites show up from the year they were built or founded, and tapping a dot opens its card.

134 real inventions and things people made, at the place and year they first appeared: from 3.3-million-year-old stone tools at Lomekwi, the Pesse canoe and the first alphabet to Gutenberg's press, the Iron Bridge, ARPANET and the first text message. 87 are new events with their own short scene and collectible Invention cards; 47 give older milestones like the telephone and the Wright Flyer their real place, a fact and a source

Lakes change with history: reservoirs like Lake Volta, Lake Nasser and Lake Mead fill in the years their dams closed, the Aral Sea shrinks from 1960, Lake Chad from 1963, Lake Texcoco drains around Mexico City, and the Great Lakes disappear under the ice-age ice sheets

Sky events: 218 real eclipses, comets, supernovae, transits of Venus, great aurorae and meteor storms. Watch the Moon's shadow cross the real path of every total solar eclipse from 1900 to 2100 (NASA predictions for the future ones), aurorae spread toward the tropics in the Carrington Event, and Halley's Comet return through history.

Whales and dolphins come up to breathe: humpbacks and blue whales rise, blow misty spouts and dive again (humpbacks lift their flukes for deep dives), orcas surface for a single breath between short dives, and dolphins pop up every 20 to 40 seconds. Tap one to see if it is diving or breathing
Fact check: city populations in the past no longer shrink Europe, North America and Japan too hard (Madrid 1969 now about 2.6M, not 0.9M); Orellana's Amazon journey starts in December 1541

Night looks like night: trees, animals and buildings on the dark side of the planet no longer catch sunlight through the Earth, and fade into moonlit silhouettes at dusk. Event alerts now appear below the date panel instead of on top of it

748 more real animals from the last 6 million years of the dinosaur age, each living only where and when its fossils were found (Paleobiology Database): over 130 more dinosaurs, 40 pterosaurs, mosasaurs and plesiosaurs, crocodile relatives, turtles, lizards and snakes, early mammals, birds, frogs and salamanders, and hundreds of sharks, rays and fish. The high Cretaceous seas now flood the lowlands, as they really did: Florida and the Gulf coast are underwater and the inland seaway is wider. Storms no longer get modern names before people named them.

Wildfires now leave a trail of black ash, tell you what is burning and why, and animals run from the flames. 51 more lost species on their real last-seen dates and places, from the dusky seaside sparrow to the Lake Pedder earthworm, each with its source

319 more real species interactions, from Nemegt tyrannosaurs and Madagascar's abelisaurs to sabre-cats, terror birds, dodo nest raiders and guard llamas. New: herds close into a defensive ring when a predator comes near, like muskoxen against wolves and elephants around their calves.

Dinosaurs look like themselves: T. rex and other two-legged dinosaurs now lean forward with a deep skull, long tapering tail, big thighs and tiny arms; Triceratops gets its huge head, swept-back frill, two long brow horns and a beak

Night-side city lights now glow by size: big metros shine wider and brighter from space while small towns stay pinpricks. Countdown labels for upcoming events no longer pile on top of each other when two land on the same city, the "Add to album" button after opening a card pack works again on iPhone, and planes and ships cost less to animate.

Sharper mountains up close: fly low over the Himalaya, the Alps, the Andes, the Rockies or the East African Rift and the ground now shows the real ridges and valleys, from NOAA's ETOPO1 elevation data at 4 arc-minutes (about 7 km), loaded only when you get close.

35 more real animals and 16 fossil plants, each placed at its real fossil sites from the Paleobiology Database: Shantungosaurus and Mononykus in Asia, Thalassotitan and Phosphatodraco off Morocco, Pycnonemosaurus and Lestodon in South America, the thylacine and Quinkana in Australia, Llanocetus in Antarctica, plus kauri, tree ferns, Eucalyptus, beech and more. 30 older species also got their real fossil sites.

Card leaderboards (Top tab): top collectors this season and all time, the luckiest low serial numbers, and who found each card first. Share any view with 🔗 in the Now panel: the link opens right at that spot. On computers, menus now open as a side panel. Added a privacy policy and terms of use, and the world and everyone's cards are now backed up every night.

Cities now rise in their real founding years: about 5,800 cities carry their founding date or first written record from Wikidata, so Brasília appears in 1960, Saint Petersburg in 1703, Johannesburg in 1886, Chicago in 1837 and Berlin in the 1200s instead of everything being there from the start. Young cities show when they were founded on their label, and 440 big cities get a founding moment in Happening now.
Fact check: New Zealand's first settlement now dated about AD 1250-1300 and Hannibal's army numbers corrected.

328 more real animal interactions from field studies and fossils: cheetahs dodging lions, baboons and elephants mobbing predators, vultures and condors circling carcasses, cleaner fish at mantas and turtles, humpbacks mobbing killer whales, Ice Age cave lions, sabre-tooths and dire wolves, and tyrannosaur and mosasaur prey

New ⚙️ Settings: name tags, map names, clouds, sound, battery saver, card notes, compact panel, side buttons and °F/°C in one place. Every card you find now has a serial number (#1 is the first one anyone found), and spotting a card shows a small note instead of a full-screen pop-up.

Herds keep their distance from predators and move off when one comes close. Zoom out to see the continents, oceans and seas as they were at the time: Laramidia, Appalachia and the Western Interior Seaway in the dinosaur age, Doggerland and the Bering land bridge in the Ice Age. Tap ▾ on the date panel and ⋯ on the side buttons to free up the screen. Pterosaurs now stick to coasts and inland seas.

Airliners now climb out, cruise and descend into their destination at real heights for their era, pitch up and down, wait at the gate, and mostly stay grounded at night; tap a plane to see what it's doing
More natural nights: after sunset the land, trees, animals and buildings fall into a dim, cool moonlight instead of glowing, with a gentle twilight in between, so city lights and campfires stand out.

46 great animal migrations now follow their real routes through the real seasons of every sim year: wildebeest around the Serengeti, caribou to the Arctic coast, Arctic terns pole to pole, godwits nonstop across the Pacific, monarchs to Mexico, gray whales to Baja, eels to the Sargasso Sea, red crabs to the sea on Christmas Island and more. Fly close to see the herd, flock or pod and its route; tap the label for distance, numbers and the tracking study behind it. Migrations under way are listed in Happening now.

Predators clash too: rival tyrannosaurs face-bite over territory, bigger hunters chase smaller ones off their kills, and a new web of real, researched interactions shapes who hunts, scavenges, follows and avoids whom, from T. rex and Edmontosaurus to lions, hyenas, vultures, wolves and elk.

Smoother when looking at cities: night lights and city names no longer recheck all 34,000 cities twice a second. Long plant and animal names now fit on screen instead of running off the edge, and the same plant isn't labelled over and over.
Herbivores fight back: horned and armoured dinosaurs and the biggest long-necks stand their ground and usually drive predators off, just as healed bite wounds in real fossils show they sometimes did.

About 2,000 real battles, sieges and sea battles from 1457 BCE to 2024 now happen on their real dates and at their real places. Fly close to see each one marked on the map; the best-known ones also pop up as alerts. Tap one for what war it was part of, who took part, and how exactly its date is known (from Wikidata).

Wildlife feels alive: herbivores graze with heads down, long-necked giants browse treetops, predators that make a catch stop to eat while the carcass lies where it fell, sharks and sea reptiles hunt fish, and animals leave dung behind. Tap any animal to see what it's doing.

Trading cards! Every era is a season: collect its animals, plants, wonders and events while it plays, because once the era passes its cards can only be traded. Free pack every day, spot animals for their cards, and be there live for event cards. Animals now live in herds, predators keep their own territory, and most animals sleep at night. Tapping something shows one card that stays put; tap again to close it.

Snow on mountain tops: the snow line follows real latitudes (about 5 km up near the equator, 3 km in the Alps, 1.5 km in Norway), drops in winter and in ice ages and rises as the climate warms. Sharper land up close with fine ground detail. Weather now updates as soon as you fly somewhere new.

86 real milestones from the last dinosaurs to the first humans now appear on the timeline at their real dates and fossil sites: the Wonderchicken, Titanoboa, the first penguins, bats, whales, cats and apes, Laetoli's footprints, heat spikes, a second asteroid off West Africa and more. Each card says what the fossils show and which study found it, and deep-time events now fly to where the place was on the drifting continents.

Smoother on phones: far-away trees, people and animals are no longer drawn when they would be smaller than a pixel, cutting the work per frame roughly in half. Mountains, ridges and valleys are now shaded so the terrain stands out, the biome colours blend instead of showing blocks, and rivers are brighter.

Every prehistoric animal checked against the Paleobiology Database: each now lives only near real fossil sites of about its age, and a few wrong dates are fixed (the cave lion and steppe bison no longer survive to today). 30 new real animals, from Ornithomimus and Austroraptor to Hesperocyon, the American mastodon and the straight-tusked elephant; 10 kinds of insects; and 17 real fossil plants, from dawn redwoods and nipa palms to southern beech, growing where their fossils were found.

Tour now glides from place to place every 20 seconds, never repeating nearby spots, with a card saying where you are and what lives there: tap Stay here to keep a spot or Next to move on. Crocodiles now live only on warm coasts and wetlands near real crocodile fossil sites. Tap any plant for its card. Fixed a panel peeking out under the buttons.

828 real volcanic eruptions and 817 historic tsunamis from NOAA's hazard databases, on their real dates and places: the deadliest erupt and send waves across the ocean, and earthquake cards now show how high their tsunami reached

The oceans now have their real depths: shallow shelves glow pale, the deep basins go dark and trenches like the Mariana are nearly black. Up close, the seafloor is shaped in 3D under see-through water, with ridges and trenches you can see.

The website now shares one world: everyone sees the same people and the same history. Now at humanitylivewatch.com. New first-visit walkthrough (replay it from the clock panel), a report button in chat, a 13+ check before posting, a privacy page, and a proper preview card when you share the link.

About 2,700 real significant earthquakes from 2150 BCE to today, from NOAA's global database: each strikes on its real date and place. The deadliest and biggest shake the globe; tap any for its toll, shaking, houses lost and whether it raised a tsunami.
